Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications

sorting DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine) histories into contraindication, precaution or neither · the vaccines each visit allows and the age windows that open and closeIs the window open, and is there a named reason this child cannot have it?

Bottom line
  • Two checks at every visit: has the vaccine's age window opened for this child, and has it closed? If it is open, vaccinate unless you can name a contraindication or precaution; a history that only sounds disqualifying is neither.
  • DTaP (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis) is contraindicated by anaphylaxis after a previous dose or to a component (no further doses of any component), or after encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose and with no other cause, which bars only the pertussis part: finish with DT (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids). Precautions defer the dose unless the benefit outweighs the risk: a progressive or unstable neurologic disorder, such as uncontrolled seizures, or a moderate or severe acute illness; a cold with low fever is neither.
  • Rotavirus vaccine is live and oral: never after intussusception or with SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency); the first dose by 14 weeks 6 days, no dose after 8 months 0 days. Up to date at 4 months: second doses are due of rotavirus, IPV (inactivated poliovirus vaccine), PCV (pneumococcal conjugate vaccine), Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) and DTaP; influenza waits for 6 months, MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) and varicella for 12 months.

A contraindication means the vaccine is not given; a precaution means defer in general, though the vaccine may still be given if its benefit is greater than its risk, for example during an outbreak; neither means vaccinate today. Live vaccines add two bars, both in the child being vaccinated: pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency.

DTaP: contraindication, precaution or neither
CategoryHistories
Contraindication (any vaccine with pertussis)Anaphylaxis after a previous dose or to a component, so no further doses of any component · Encephalopathy within 7 days of a dose (coma, a lowered level of consciousness or prolonged seizures), with no other cause: give DT
Precaution (defer or weigh)Moderate or severe illnessModerate or severe illness: a significant fever, over 39 °C, or a severe illness without fever; it delays the dose, while a cold, even with low fever, does not. · Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks of a tetanus-toxoid dose · A progressive or unstable neurologic disorder (infantile spasms, uncontrolled epilepsy or progressive encephalopathy): the pertussis part waits until neurologic status is clarified and stable · Arthus-type reaction to a diphtheria- or tetanus-toxoid dose: wait at least 10 years from the last tetanus-toxoid dose
Neither (vaccinate today)Reactions to an earlier dose: fever of 40.5 °C or higher within the first 48 hours; in the same 48 hours, a collapse or shock-like state (hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode) or 3 hours or more of inconsolable crying; a seizure in the first 3 days The MSD Manual and older sources, the earlier version of this brief among them, list these four reactions as precautions, whereas current guidance from the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) names them among conditions incorrectly perceived as contraindications or precautions. · Family history of seizures or epilepsy; a neurologic condition that is stable or has resolved; the child's own febrile seizure · A mild illness, low fever included; a recent exposure to an infection
Other routine vaccines: when not to give
VaccineDo not giveDefer
Rotavirus (live, oral) The vaccine enlarges the Peyer patches, which can act as a lead point; the risk rises with age, hence the early first dose and the cutoff at 8 months 0 days.SCID; any past intussusception; anaphylaxis to a dose or a componentModerate or severe illness, including moderate or severe vomiting or diarrhea; altered immunity other than SCID
MMR and varicella (live, injected)Pregnancy or severe immunodeficiency in the child being vaccinated Moderate or severe illness; blood products containing antibody within the past 11 months (the interval depends on the product)
Nasal influenza (LAIV, live attenuated influenza vaccine)Under 2 years; aspirin or other salicylate therapy; immunocompromise; pregnancy; caring for a severely immunocompromised person in a protected environmentGive the injected inactivated vaccine instead, from 6 months
Histories that do not stop vaccination
HistoryRuling
A cold or other mild illness, even with low feverVaccinate today; moderate or severe illness is the precaution
Egg allergyAny influenza vaccine appropriate for age
BreastfeedingNot a contraindication
Pregnancy in the mother or another household contactGive MMR and varicella to the child: pregnancy bars live vaccines only in the person vaccinated
Current antibiotics, or preterm birthVaccinate; hepatitis B vaccine is an exception in some preterm infants
Penicillin or another nonvaccine allergy, or relatives with allergiesVaccinate
An immunosuppressed household contactVaccinate; varicella is recommended for such contacts, and nasal influenza is avoided only beside a protected environment
Fever and a mild rash 1 to 3 weeks after MMRVaccine-strain reaction: reassure
Age windows that open or close
VaccineWindowDoses
RotavirusDose 1 between 2 months and 14 weeks 6 days, never on or after 15 weeks 0 days; nothing after 8 months 0 daysTwo doses of RV1 (monovalent), at 2 and 4 months, or three of RV5 (pentavalent), at 2, 4 and 6 months
InfluenzaEach season, starting at 6 monthsAges 6 months to 8 years in a first season (fewer than 2 earlier doses, or history unknown): 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart
MMR and varicellaFirst doses at 12 to 15 months and second doses at 4 to 6 yearsLive injected vaccines: the same day or at least 4 weeks apart
Vaccines due at each visit
VisitVaccines dueAge limit that matters
2 monthsFirst doses of DTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirus; the second hepatitis B dose (the first is given at birth) unless it was given at 1 monthThe first rotavirus dose cannot wait past 14 weeks 6 days
4 monthsSecond doses of the same five: DTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirusInfluenza opens at 6 months; MMR and varicella at 12 months
6 monthsThird doses of DTaP and PCV; a third Hib dose unless the series used PedvaxHIB; a third rotavirus dose only with RV5; hepatitis B and IPV third doses, due between 6 and 18 months; influenza when in seasonNo rotavirus after 8 months 0 days; a first influenza season takes 2 doses
12 to 15 monthsFirst MMR and varicella doses; hepatitis A, the first of 2 doses, given at 12 to 23 months; the fourth PCV dose and the Hib boosterThe live injected vaccines open at 12 months
15 to 18 monthsDTaP fourth doseNo closing window
4 to 6 yearsDTaP fifth dose; IPV, MMR and varicella last dosesBefore school entry; then Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis booster) from 11 years
Which childhood vaccines are live
ClassVaccines
Live attenuatedRotavirus, MMR, varicella; also nasal influenza, BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) and oral polio, which the United States no longer uses
Inactivated (killed)IPV and injected influenza
ToxoidDiphtheria and tetanus
Subunit or conjugateAcellular pertussis, Hib and pneumococcal conjugate
Pause point
Brief seizure the evening after the last DTaP dose, well since Offered as precaution or switch to DT Was it encephalopathy within 7 days, or an unstable disorder? → Neither: a seizure within 3 days of a dose does not bar DTaP; vaccinate today
Past 15 weeks old, starting vaccines, no rotavirus yet Offered as rotavirus today or rotavirus at the next visit Has the window for the first rotavirus dose closed? → Yes, after 14 weeks 6 days: give the other 2-month vaccines without rotavirus
Egg allergy with hives, due for influenza vaccine Offered as skip influenza vaccine or an egg-free vaccine only Does egg allergy bar any influenza vaccine? → No: any influenza vaccine appropriate for age
Practice
  1. 2-month-old boy is at the well-child visit for his first vaccines His father has epilepsy, and an older sister had seizures with fever His mother asks to skip the pertussis vaccine development and examination normal T 36.9 °C · HR 140/min → Neither → a family history of seizures or epilepsy is neither a contraindication nor a precaution: vaccinate today. The mother's request is a matter for counseling; it does not change the classification
  2. 6-month-old boy is brought for his third DTaP dose Two days after his 4-month dose he was hard to arouse and had a prolonged seizure Evaluation found no other cause T 36.8 °C · HR 128/min alert and interactive today → Contraindication → decreased consciousness and a prolonged seizure within 7 days of a previous dose, with no other cause, is the encephalopathy that contraindicates every pertussis-containing vaccine: complete the series with DT. A precaution is weighed; this is not
  3. 17-week-old boy is starting his infant vaccines today His family moved from another state He received only the hepatitis B birth dose growth and examination normal T 36.9 °C · HR 138/min → Rotavirus vaccine → the rotavirus series cannot start on or after 15 weeks 0 days (first dose by 14 weeks 6 days), so it is never given to him. DTaP and the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine are 2-month vaccines he is due for
  4. 4-month-old girl is due for her 4-month vaccines Runny nose and mild cough for 2 days; feeding well playful; clear nasal discharge; lungs clear T 38.1 °C · HR 150/min · respirations 40/min → Neither → a mild acute illness, with or without fever, is neither: vaccinate today. Moderate or severe acute illness is the precaution
  5. 12-month-old boy is at his well-child visit with his mother She is 20 weeks pregnant and asks whether his vaccines could harm the fetus Healthy; up to date on infant vaccines examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 118/min → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines today → the CDC lists pregnancy of the recipient's mother or another close or household contact as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution for both vaccines. Pregnancy contraindicates them only in the person being vaccinated, so neither is deferred
  6. 6-month-old girl is brought for her third DTaP dose Clusters of sudden flexion spasms began 3 weeks ago and continue daily despite treatment She has lost the ability to roll over T 36.8 °C · HR 122/min → Precaution → infantile spasms are a progressive neurologic disorder: a precaution, so defer DTaP until neurologic status is clarified and stable. A brief seizure within 3 days of a dose, or a stable neurologic condition, would be neither
  7. 7-month-old girl is at a well-child visit in November Up to date on her infant vaccines She has never received influenza vaccine growth and examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 130/min → Influenza vaccine today and a second dose in 4 weeks → influenza vaccine starts at 6 months, every season; a child aged 6 months to 8 years with fewer than 2 earlier doses, or an unknown history, gets 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart. Waiting for the 12-month visit misses this season
  8. 6-month-old girl is brought for her third DTaP dose The night after her 4-month dose her temperature reached 41 °C; it resolved within a day No seizure; well since then T 36.7 °C · HR 125/min → Neither → fever of 40.5 °C or higher within 48 hours of a previous dose is listed by the CDC as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution: vaccinate today. Older sources called it a precaution
  9. 12-month-old girl returns 2 weeks after her 12-month visit She received measles-mumps-rubella vaccine at that visit; varicella vaccine was out of stock Healthy; no immune problems examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 120/min → Varicella vaccine in 2 weeks → injected live vaccines not given on the same day need at least 4 weeks between them; varicella vaccine given today, 2 weeks after measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, would not count and would have to be repeated at least 4 weeks later. Waiting until 4 to 6 years skips the first varicella dose, due at 12 to 15 months
  10. 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Within 10 minutes of her 2-month dose she developed hives, wheezing and low blood pressure She received epinephrine in the clinic T 37.0 °C · HR 132/min → Contraindication → hives, wheezing and hypotension within minutes of a dose is anaphylaxis: a severe allergic reaction after a previous dose or to a vaccine component contraindicates that vaccine
  11. 12-month-old boy is at a well-child visit Up to date on his vaccines, including the rotavirus series Healthy, with normal growth and development examination normal; no immune problems T 36.7 °C · HR 118/min → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella → MMR and varicella are the live injected vaccines first given at 12 to 15 months, with second doses at 4 to 6 years; the rotavirus series ended by 8 months 0 days
  12. 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Six hours after her 2-month dose she had a brief seizure that stopped on its own Since then she has been well, with normal development T 37.0 °C · HR 135/min → Neither → a seizure within 3 days of a previous dose is listed by the CDC as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution: vaccinate today. Older sources called it a precaution. Uncontrolled seizures or a progressive neurologic disorder would be the precaution
  13. 4-month-old boy is due for his 4-month vaccines Admitted yesterday with pneumonia; needs supplemental oxygen tachypneic with right-sided crackles T 39.2 °C · HR 170/min · oxygen saturation 91% on room air → Precaution → a moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever, is a precaution: in general defer until he recovers. A mild illness, such as a cold with low fever, is neither
Schedule status, October 2026 In January 2026 the CDC moved childhood rotavirus and influenza vaccines from routine to shared clinical decision-making. A federal court stayed that change in March 2026, and the stay is under appeal. The schedule CDC now posts is the 2025 schedule, which lists both vaccines as routine; check the CDC site for the current schedule. The AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) publishes its own schedule and opposed the change, and the NBME item keys rotavirus as a routine 4-month vaccine.
How NBME framed it: question 1

4-month-old girl at a well-child visit in October Uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery; vaccines up to date Normal growth and development for age vital signs normal normal examination

Immunization against which disease is most appropriate at this time?

Competing answers
  • Chickenpox: a routine live childhood vaccine; but the first varicella dose is not given until 12 months.
  • Measles-mumps-rubella: routine and live, like rotavirus; but the first dose is at 12 months.
  • Shingles: the same virus as chickenpox; but zoster vaccine is for adults from age 50; the NBME explanation, an older source, says 60.

Down to two: rotavirus or influenza. Rotavirus: up to date at 4 months means the 2-month doses were given, so the second doses are due, rotavirus among them. The October date is a seasonal cue for influenza, but at 4 months she is below its 6-month age limit. The options form an age ladder, from rotavirus at 2 months through MMR and varicella at 12 months to zoster at 50.

Pairs with Adolescent Vaccines covers the 11 to 12 year visit and influenza timing by season.
Vaccines in Special Populations covers live vaccines in HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), asplenia and immunodeficiency.
Vaccines in Pregnancy covers Tdap and influenza in pregnancy and the live vaccines it bars.
Anaphylaxis covers treating a severe allergic reaction to a vaccine.
Transferable rule

Check the child's age against each vaccine's age window before the season or the disease; a vaccine whose window has not opened, or has closed, is not given at this visit. Then vaccinate unless you can name the criterion that makes the child ineligible.
